faq.a: Long‑acting reversible contraception (IUDs and implants) offers the highest efficacy and low user‑error rates.
faq.q: What is the most effective contraceptive method in low‑resource settings?

faq.a: Yes, condoms provide STI protection and can be used concurrently with hormonal or LARC methods.
faq.q: Can I use condoms with other methods?

faq.a: Combined oral contraceptives are acceptable with most antiretrovirals; avoid methods that interact with protease inhibitors.
faq.q: What should I do if a patient has HIV and wants a contraceptive?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with HIV on efavirenz wants to avoid pregnancy. — Discuss MEC Class 1 for COCs, explain drug interaction, and offer LARC as alternative.
A 35‑year‑old woman presents with heavy bleeding after IUD insertion. — Identify possible expulsion or infection, order ultrasound if available, and plan removal or replacement.
A 22‑year‑old patient reports missed pills and unintended pregnancy. — Explain typical‑use failure, counsel on backup methods, and discuss emergency contraception.
A 30‑year‑old woman with anemia wants a contraceptive. — Choose a method that does not worsen menstrual bleeding; consider implant or copper IUD.
A 40‑year‑old woman with a history of TB wants contraception. — Discuss contraindications of hormonal methods during active TB treatment and recommend LARC.
A 25‑year‑old woman with a history of breast cancer wants contraception. — Explain MEC Class 4 for hormonal methods and recommend non‑hormonal options like copper IUD.
A 18‑year‑old patient wants emergency contraception after unprotected sex. — Choose levonorgestrel or ulipristal based on timing, explain efficacy limits, and counsel on future FP.
ai.title: Family Planning in Low-Resource Settings
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Clinicians must assess reproductive goals, risk factors, and local constraints to counsel patients on effective, safe contraceptive methods. Practical skills include history taking, method selection, and managing complications.

b: Key goals: avoid unintended pregnancy, improve maternal health, empower women
sections.p: Family planning (FP) refers to the use of contraceptive methods to achieve desired spacing or limiting of pregnancies. In low‑resource settings, FP reduces maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality.

b: Efficacy: perfect use vs typical use; failure rates; method-specific contraindications
sections.p: Effective FP requires understanding of method efficacy, contraindications, and local availability. The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) classifies methods by safety in specific conditions.

t.b: Measures population uptake; high rates indicate successful FP programs.

b: Screen for HIV, TB, malaria, anemia; these influence method choice
sections.p: Unintended pregnancies in East Africa are linked to higher rates of unsafe abortions, maternal anaemia, and neonatal complications. Clinicians must integrate FP into routine antenatal and post‑partum care.

t.b: Rule out pregnancy before prescribing hormonal methods; a positive result indicates need for pregnancy termination or safe abortion.
Identify anaemia; iron deficiency may contraindicate certain progestin‑only methods due to menstrual changes.
Determine need for combined oral contraceptives (COCs) with antiretroviral therapy; avoid drug interactions.

b: Remember MEC Class 1: no restriction; Class 2: advantage outweighs risk; Class 3: risk outweighs advantage; Class 4: contraindicated
sections.p: Examiners often ask about method selection in specific scenarios and the management of side effects. Focus on MEC classes and local resource constraints.

b: Assuming all patients can access long‑acting reversible contraception (LARC)
sections.p: Over‑reliance on perfect‑use efficacy, neglecting typical‑use failure, and ignoring local availability of methods.

b: LARC (IUD, implant) preferred for high efficacy and low compliance
sections.p: Choose method based on patient preference, medical history, and availability. Provide counseling, prescribe, and arrange follow‑up.

t.b: Ask about menstrual history, infections, and contraindications; explain pain management and follow‑up.
Assess for expulsion, infection, or side effects; remove if complications arise.

b: Emergency contraception is a short‑term, high‑dose method; FP is ongoing.
sections.p: Distinguish FP from emergency contraception and from fertility awareness methods.

b: Repeat pregnancy test if clinical suspicion remains
sections.p: False‑negative pregnancy tests in early pregnancy; low haemoglobin may mask anemia; rapid HIV tests may miss early seroconversion.
Use simple, affordable tests to guide method choice and detect contraindications.

t.b: Rule out pregnancy before hormonal methods; a positive result indicates need for abortion services.
Identify anaemia; severe anaemia may contraindicate progestin‑only methods.
Screen for HIV; positive status influences choice of COCs and requires counseling.
Screen for STIs; treat before initiating hormonal methods to avoid complications.
